To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) violations of single-peaked preferences are not rare, 2) the violations are significantly larger in the presence of other-regarding preferences and in the presence of equal-split, and 3) the violations cannot be attributed to the ease of reporting certain preference rankings or to errors.

other-regarding preferences are not single-peaked or plateaued in the vast majority of subjects and the presence of the equal split in the set of available options increases the number of such violations.

(a) subjects violate single-peakness in the ordinal preference rankings of outcomes in decision tasks based in the dictator and trust games, (b) the violations of single-peaked preferences are more prevalent in other-regarding subjects and in the presence of an equal-split option, and (c) the violations cannot be attributed to ease of reporting certain ordinal rankings or as errors in reporting the ordinal rankings of the theoretical benchmark.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the empirical validity of a theoretical assumption that is common to a wide class of models.
the empirical testing of the single-peakedness assumption in the theory of other-regarding preferences.
the question of whether the preferences of other-regarding subjects are consistent with a single-peakedness assumption.

there are violations but the evidence does not allow us to determine whether the violations are systematic and significant.
other-regarding preferences are not necessarily single-peaked.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the single-peakedness assumption is not a robust feature of outcome-based other regarding preferences.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the single-peakedness of other-regarding preferences is not as strong as is commonly assumed in the literature.
other-regarding preferences are more likely to be single-plateau rather than single-peaked, and that this is true even for preferences that are based on material payoffs.
the single-peakedness assumption is not robust to the experimental setting and that it should be used with caution in empirical studies of other-regarding preferences.
